item.title: Fiji must create job creators, not just job seekers – RBF Governor
item.description: Reserve Bank of Fiji Governor Ariff Ali says Fiji must create an environment where young people can become job creators rather than simply job seekers as the country looks to innovation to diversify its economy. Speaking at the opening of the Fiji Innovation Hub Space yesterday, Ali said Fiji could not continue relying indefinitely on a narrow range of economic activities and needed to develop new
item.content:encoded:
Reserve Bank of Fiji Governor Ariff Ali says Fiji must create an environment where young people can become job creators rather than simply job seekers as the country looks to innovation to diversify its economy.

Speaking at the opening of the Fiji Innovation Hub Space yesterday, Ali said Fiji could not continue relying indefinitely on a narrow range of economic activities and needed to develop new sources of growth.

“We need to broaden the sources of economic growth and create more opportunities for our people. We need to diversify our economy,” Ali said.

He said technology was rapidly changing the economic and financial landscape, transforming how people save, borrow, invest, make payments and conduct business.

Ali said the Reserve Bank operated at an important intersection of the economy and could not operate separately from the broader changes taking place.

At the same time, he said Fiji continued to face fundamental economic challenges that required greater entrepreneurship, productivity and competitiveness.

“We need to encourage entrepreneurship. We need to develop new industries and new business models. We need to increase productivity and competitiveness,” he said.

Ali said innovation was no longer simply desirable but had become necessary for Fiji’s economic development.

A major motivation behind the Innovation Hub, he said, was creating greater opportunities for young Fijians to participate meaningfully in the economy.

“Every year, thousands of Fijians leave our schools and tertiary institutions with aspirations for a better future,” Ali said.

“We should, of course, continue creating good jobs. But we should also create an environment where our young people can become job creators, not just job seekers.”

Ali said this was the type of environment the new Fiji Innovation Hub Space was intended to help foster.

item.title: Minister Ditoka holds talks in Seoul on energy, climate cooperation
item.description: Foreign Affairs Minister Sakiasi Ditoka has held talks with his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun in Seoul, with discussions focusing on strengthening bilateral relations, energy security and climate change cooperation. Ditoka is currently visiting South Korea as Fiji and Korea mark the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries.
item.content:encoded:
Foreign Affairs Minister Sakiasi Ditoka has held talks with his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun in Seoul, with discussions focusing on strengthening bilateral relations, energy security and climate change cooperation.

Ditoka is currently visiting South Korea as Fiji and Korea mark the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries.

His visit is also the first by a Fijian foreign minister to Seoul since September 2015.

During talks yesterday, Ditoka expressed Fiji’s interest in deepening cooperation with South Korea on energy supply chains amid growing concerns over global energy security.

He highlighted the impact of the volatile security situation in the Strait of Hormuz on countries across the Asia-Pacific region.

Cho agreed that establishing stable and resilient energy supply chains had become increasingly important.

The two ministers agreed to deepen cooperation in this area and maintain close consultations on energy security.

Discussions also covered South Korea’s cooperation with Fiji in healthcare and energy.

Cho said Seoul had been working to expand its engagement with Fiji in areas regarded as particularly valuable to the country.

Ditoka thanked South Korea for its assistance and sought continued engagement, particularly in addressing climate change.

The ministers also exchanged views on the security situation on the Korean Peninsula and its wider implications for the Pacific region.

They agreed to work together on consular matters, including efforts to protect South Korean nationals in Fiji.

The talks come as Fiji and South Korea seek to strengthen a diplomatic relationship spanning more than five decades.

item.title: Charters’ lawyers cite constitutional protection for journalistic sources
item.description: Lawyers for journalist and sports marketing expert Charlie Charters will tell the High Court that the confidentiality of journalistic sources is protected by Fiji’s Constitution and common law, as they challenge the re-seizure of his electronic devices. Fatiaki Law has filed the High Court application following the re-seizure of seven devices which Charters says contain confidential journalistic m
item.content:encoded:
Lawyers for journalist and sports marketing expert Charlie Charters will tell the High Court that the confidentiality of journalistic sources is protected by Fiji’s Constitution and common law, as they challenge the re-seizure of his electronic devices.

Fatiaki Law has filed the High Court application following the re-seizure of seven devices which Charters says contain confidential journalistic material, information capable of identifying sources and communications with his legal advisers.

Central to the application is the protection afforded to journalists and their sources.

“The confidentiality of journalistic sources is protected by sections 17 and 24 of the Constitution and at common law,” the application states.

Charters’ lawyers also rely on findings made by the High Court in its July 24 ruling in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. HAM 12 of 2026.

The application argues there is a valid legal claim for the devices and their contents to be treated as privileged or confidential because they are Charters’ personal electronic devices and contain material obtained or received in the course of his journalism.

It says the material includes communications and information “capable of identifying the persons with whom he has so communicated”.

The lawyers argue Charters cannot identify those individuals or provide particulars of the confidential material without defeating the very confidentiality he is asking the court to protect.

Fatiaki Law also says a claim of privilege and confidentiality was made at the time of seizure and that the seizing officer was provided with a copy of section 103 of the Criminal Procedure Act 2009.

According to the application, because the electronic devices record and store information, they constitute documents for the purposes of section 103.

The lawyers contend that once the claim was made, section 103(2) required the person holding the devices to seal them and have them delivered to the Registrar of the High Court.

The application says Charters is unaware of any compliance with that requirement.

His lawyers have also raised questions about the latest search warrant, claiming both the Information to Obtain a Search Warrant and the warrant itself are undated.

They further claim the documents do not identify any particular investigation or provide details capable of informing Charters of the legal and factual basis on which the warrant was obtained.

The High Court application follows the re-seizure of the devices after Police had earlier been ordered to return them to Charters’ lawyer.

The claims concerning privilege, confidentiality and the validity and execution of the latest seizure are now matters before the High Court.

item.title: Devices returned, then seized again – Charters files case against Police
item.description: Journalist and sports marketing expert Charlie Charters has filed a High Court motion after seven electronic devices seized during an investigation were returned to his lawyer and then immediately re-seized by Fiji Police under a fresh court order. In a statement, Charters said the development occurred on Friday after his lawyer, Seforan Fatiaki, went to the Criminal Investigations Department foll
item.content:encoded:
Journalist and sports marketing expert Charlie Charters has filed a High Court motion after seven electronic devices seized during an investigation were returned to his lawyer and then immediately re-seized by Fiji Police under a fresh court order.

In a statement, Charters said the development occurred on Friday after his lawyer, Seforan Fatiaki, went to the Criminal Investigations Department following a Magistrates Court order for the devices to be returned.

“You’ve always got to be braced for Fiji’s capacity to surprise. But even we were shocked by what happened to my lawyer Mr Seforan Fatiaki when he presented himself to CID on Friday,” Charters said.

According to Charters, Magistrate Shageeth Somaratne had earlier that day ordered Police to return the seven devices to Fatiaki.

Charters said Police produced the devices to his lawyer that afternoon but simultaneously served him with a fresh seizure order.

“So, on Friday afternoon Police produced the seven devices to show to Mr Fatiaki as instructed, and in the same instant Mr Fatiaki was then served with a fresh seizure order by Police who still have the devices,” he said.

The devices were originally seized following Charters’ detention and arrest in February as part of an investigation by the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption.

Charges subsequently brought against Charters were permanently stayed by the High Court on July 24.

Charters said his lawyer had initially written to FICAC on March 16 seeking the return of the devices.

He questioned the latest seizure, arguing that the High Court ruling had addressed important constitutional protections.

“The Police do not appear to have understood Justice Bulamainaivalu’s ruling,” Charters said.

“The charges against me were stayed by the High Court for a number of reasons including that, in the absence of any law limiting my rights, we all enjoy the right of freedom of speech, expression, thought, opinion and publication under section 17 of the Constitution.”

Charters also referred to protections concerning journalistic sources, saying the High Court had recognised the right not to divulge sources of journalistic information when exercising those constitutional rights.

He said the latest development raised broader concerns despite what he described as progress by the Government in restoring media freedom.

“Anyone who follows my writing on Facebook will know that I am always at great pains to give credit to this Government for helping to restore something like media freedom,” he said.

“But this raises a huge number of frankly uncomfortable questions and casts a long shadow on the Government’s record.”

Charters also alleged there were significant errors in documentation relating to the search warrant. He said those matters would form part of submissions in the new High Court proceedings.

The allegations and characterisations in Charters’ statement are his own. Police and FICAC have not been quoted in the statement responding to the claims surrounding the latest seizure.

National airline flies Cure Kids
item.description: NATIONAL airline Fiji Airways is helping Cure Kids Fiji extend healthcare programs, specialist training and research to communities nationwide, including remote maritime areas. Managing director and chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the partnership reflected the airline’s commitment to supporting communities.
item.content:encoded:
NATIONAL airline Fiji Airways is helping Cure Kids Fiji extend healthcare programs, specialist training and research to communities nationwide, including remote maritime areas.

Managing director and chief executive officer Paul Scurrah said the partnership reflected the airline’s commitment to supporting communities.

“In a country of scattered islands, air travel is a lifeline, not a luxury,” Mr Scurrah said.

“Through our partnership with Cure Kids Fiji, we’re using that lifeline to help bring life-saving care closer to the children who need it.”

Since the partnership began, Fiji Airways has supported 41 flight sectors — 30 domestic and 11 international — enabling healthcare professionals, program staff, specialists and researchers to reach communities in need.

The initiatives have reached 819 people, including 716 pregnant women through antenatal programs and 103 children through rheumatic heart disease (RHD) screening.

Fiji Airways said the impact was evident at a community health screening during the Accor Hotels Sports Day in Nadi.

“Cure Kids Fiji and the Ministry of Health and Medical Services Western Division screening team offered free heart screening to families attending the event.

“Fiji Airways-supported travel enabled a paediatric registrar from Labasa Hospital to travel to Nadi to support the outreach. A total of 103 children were screened, with several identified as having early-stage RHD.

“Children with early-stage RHD often show no symptoms and may appear healthy. Early detection allows families to receive counselling and referrals for ongoing care before the disease progresses.”

Cure Kids Fiji country manager Dr Jimaima Kailawadoko-Matanaicake said the partnership was making a real difference.

“Something as simple as providing transport can completely change a child’s future,” she said.

With Fiji Airways support, Cure Kids Fiji is strengthening national programs including RHD prevention and screening, the Fiji Antenatal Study, Strep Vaccine Global Consortium research, the Fiji Oxygen Program, and climate and respiratory health initiatives.

Travel support has also helped teams reach remote areas such as Vanuabalavu, with improvements at Lomaloma Subdivisional Hospital supporting better service delivery.

The partnership will continue to support RHD screening, specialist training and research aimed at improving health outcomes for children.

item.title: Constitutional guides
item.description: Dialogue Fiji has launched two new publications to help Fijians compare recent constitutional frameworks. The publications are Recent Constitutional Frameworks: A Comparison between the 1997 Constitution, the Ghai Draft and the 2013 Constitution, and Understanding Recent Constitutions: A Citizen’s Illustrated Guide.
item.content:encoded:
Dialogue Fiji has launched two new publications to help Fijians compare recent constitutional frameworks.

The publications are Recent Constitutional Frameworks: A Comparison between the 1997 Constitution, the Ghai Draft and the 2013 Constitution, and Understanding Recent Constitutions: A Citizen’s Illustrated Guide.

Dialogue Fiji executive director Nilesh Lal said the publications aimed to shift debate from tribal politics and personalities to knowledge of provisions, noting that the test for any constitution was in how it protected rights and how it controlled power.

Deputy Prime Minister Manoa Kamikamica said the publications did not tell readers which constitution was best and did not advocate for any amendments or replacements.

“They lay out what each constitution says, to allow citizens to compare for themselves,” Mr Kamikamica said.

“That restraint is not a weakness, it is the publication’s strength.”

He said that a constitution was a social contract, that legitimacy and public trust were inseparable from the openness of the process.

“Fiji has learned sometimes the hard way that a constitution handed out is a constitution contested, while a constitution built together is a constitution that can truly unite,” he said.

He said the process must belong to the people, not to any office, any party, or any individual, and when farmers in Tailevu, fishermen in Kadavu, market vendors in Ba and students in Suva all access the same information, the whole nation gets better.

University of the South Pacific Political Professor Dr Sandra Tarte said she found the shift from ethnic-based electoral rolls, which were a prominent feature of the 1970, 1990 and 1997 constitutions, to the common roll, which features in the Ghai Draft and the 2013 Constitution, particularly interesting.

“Also, the role of the President – from having certain legislative and executive powers under the 1997 constitution to a proposed advisory role in the Ghai Draft to being totally absent from the 2013 Constitution,” she said.

“We know of the debate around Section 131 of the 2013 Constitution which grants overall responsibility to the RFMF to ensure at all times the security, defence and well-being of Fiji and all Fijians. This has proved somewhat controversial as it may be interpreted as allowing the military a form of super constitutional authority.”

Dr Tarte said the value of the publications was that they gave Fijians the tools to make that judgment for themselves.

Both publications are now available to the public to support informed public discussion.

item.title: Tie-dye training empowers youth
item.description: YOUTH in Navosa are gaining practical tie-dye skills through a two-day training program aimed at helping them create products and explore small business opportunities. The training is being held as part of activities leading up to the Navosa Youth and Sports Festival, which will be held today and tomorrow at Vatureba Grounds in Navosa.
item.content:encoded:
YOUTH in Navosa are gaining practical tie-dye skills through a two-day training program aimed at helping them create products and explore small business opportunities.

The training is being held as part of activities leading up to the Navosa Youth and Sports Festival, which will be held today and tomorrow at Vatureba Grounds in Navosa.

Participants are learning hands-on techniques for producing tie-dye products, with the skills intended to help them develop creative and entrepreneurial opportunities within their communities.

The initiative also aims to strengthen skills of rural youth and encourage greater economic participation by providing practical knowledge that can be applied to small-scale income generating activities.

The training forms part of wider efforts to provide young people with opportunities to develop skills that can support their livelihoods and contribute to their communities.
